docs.h: The demo was never the hard part .
docs.t: AI programmes don’t fail because the model is weak. They fail in the gap between a notebook and a Tuesday afternoon — where the data won’t join, the permissions don’t exist and nobody owns the result.

The previous chapter argues you shouldn’t default to a large consultancy. That obliges us to say plainly who you get instead — including the size of us, which is the first thing a procurement team will ask.

Quenora is founder-led. The person who scopes your engagement is the person who does the work and the person you call when it breaks — there’s no account layer between the two, and no one you haven’t met ever touches the work.

Founded in 2025 by Balaji Durai. Before Quenora, he ran transformation work for multinational manufacturers, retail banking and life sciences groups — the kind of programme where several technologies have to be made to agree with each other before anything reaches a user at all.

Those systems went on to be used by more than 100,000 people, and the measure that mattered was never the launch. It was whether the working day got quieter afterwards. That’s still the test here, and it’s why one of the nine principles behind the mark is Human rather than something about models.

The firm is small, and grows by adding depth, not by hitting a headcount target. That’s a real constraint, and it shapes what we take on: single systems that need to reach production this year, not multi-year, multi-country programmes. The chapter above says the same thing from the other direction.

docs.h: Most pilots don’t fail at the model. They stop at five layers .
docs.t: A demo answers questions. A production system has to answer them for people who are allowed to ask, from data that is current, and say something useful when it does not know — while leaving a trail somebody can audit. This page walks three worked problems through the layers where that work actually stops, then sets out the governance decisions each one forces.

docs.h: Every one of them closed off an easier option.
docs.t: A principle nobody paid for is a slogan. These four are on this site, they each closed off an easier option, and the reasoning is the part worth reading.
No framework, no bundler, no build step, and not one line of script from anyone else’s server. Every page is one file: markup, styles and behaviour together.

What it cost. The hero was originally built on two well-known animation libraries served from a public CDN. On locked-down corporate networks — the exact networks our buyers sit behind — both were blocked, and the page arrived blank. Everything was rewritten against native canvas and CSS. It is the reason we are sceptical of any architecture whose first failure mode is somebody else’s uptime.
Turn scripting off and the argument is still there: every section, every answer, every link. Animation is enhancement, never the delivery mechanism.

What it cost. Reveal-on-scroll has to be written twice — once as the enhanced path and once as a default that is already visible. The one-line version is quicker to write, and leaves a blank page for anyone whose browser does not run it.

docs.h: Contrast is a build failure, not a preference
docs.t: Every text colour is checked against the surface behind it for WCAG AA. A pair that fails does not get discussed; it stops the release.

docs.h: Contrast is a build failure, not a preference
docs.t: What it cost. It rules out a lot of attractive low-contrast typography, and it caught a header button rendering at 1.49:1 — which looked fine to us and would have been unreadable to a good number of readers.

docs.h: Nothing ships unless the checks pass
docs.t: A release gate runs before every push. It is not advisory. A failing stage returns a non-zero exit code and the build is blocked.

docs.h: Nothing ships unless the checks pass
docs.t: What it cost. It is holding this site’s own release today, over two lines still to be filled in a legal page. We would rather take the extra day than ship something incomplete — the same trade we ask you to let us make on your work.

docs.h: Nothing ships unless the checks pass
docs.t: One exception, named rather than hidden. The three typefaces load from Google Fonts, which is disclosed in our privacy notice with its legal basis. Every face has a full local fallback stack, so if that request is blocked the page still sets correctly — it simply sets in a system font.
Nine stages. These are the real names and the real counts, taken from the last run — not a description of what a test suite might do.

Stage 7 is the one worth explaining, because it is the least conventional and the most revealing. The hero constellation is constructed against the page’s own six-column grid and the measured height of the headline. A test asserts that relationship at eight viewport sizes and fails the build if it breaks.

Nobody would notice a few pixels of drift. That is the point: the check exists because the alternative is a thing that is nearly right, and nearly right is how systems decay. We would rather encode the intent than rely on somebody remembering it in six months.

docs.h: Five, and what each one is tied to.
docs.t: Principles are cheap to list. Each of these is attached to something specific in how an engagement runs, so you can hold us to it.
Every phase carries an exit condition written into the statement of work. The last one is that your team runs the system without us.
A number is agreed in Phase 01. Phase 05 measures against that number in writing. If it did not move, we say so.
The code, the documentation and the evaluation harness are yours regardless of how the engagement ends. There is no scenario where you finish with nothing to show for it.

docs.h: It has to run on your estate
docs.t: Production means the systems you already have, with the permissions they already enforce. A capability that only works in a clean room has not reached the work.
The measure of a design is whether the team inheriting it can change it safely. A design only its author can maintain is a cost we would be handing you.

This is a worked example, not a case study. It describes the shape of the problem we are called into and how we take it apart, using a composite of the kind of system that stalls. No client, no numbers, nothing that happened to anybody in particular.
The setup: a retrieval assistant that answers staff questions from internal documentation. It works in the notebook. Eight months later it is still in the notebook.

A request has to clear all five to reach an answer. A pilot typically builds the first and the last, so requests stop at whichever of the middle three was skipped — and the failure looks like a bad model rather than a missing layer. Illustrative.
The documents live in four systems with four permission models. The pilot ran on an export somebody made by hand, so it never had to answer the question of who is allowed to see what.
Whether authorisation resolves per query against the source systems, or the index is partitioned by entitlement. It is the first decision and it constrains every later one.
Nobody can say whether an answer was right. The demo was judged by the people who built it, reading answers they already knew the answer to.
A test set drawn from real questions, a metric that reflects the actual cost of being wrong, and a threshold agreed before anything is built. This is the number Phase 05 measures against.
The export is a snapshot. The documentation changed the week after, and the assistant now confidently cites a policy that was withdrawn.
How change propagates: re-index on write, scheduled reconciliation, or explicit staleness shown to the reader. Each is defensible; the wrong one for the domain is how trust is lost in month three.
Asked something outside its documents, the pilot answers anyway. In a demo that reads as capability. In production it is the incident.
What the system does when it does not know — abstain, escalate to a person, or answer with the evidence attached and let the reader judge. Wired in as behaviour, not appended as a disclaimer.
It runs on somebody’s account, deploys from somebody’s laptop, and has no owner in the on-call rota. This is the layer that ends most pilots, and it is not a technical problem.
Which existing team owns it, what their runbook says, and what the alert means at three in the morning. If no team will take it, that is a finding worth more than the system.

Note what is not on that list. Which model, which vector store, which framework. Those are real decisions and they take an afternoon. The five above take the engagement, and getting them wrong is why a working demo is still a demo eight months later.
This is also why Phase 02 — the unglamorous layer — is six weeks and not one. Access, ground truth and freshness are the foundation; everything after them is comparatively cheap.

docs.h: Governance is a set of decisions, not a document.
docs.t: Most governance material describes a policy. What a production system needs is a set of answers wired into the build, because each one changes the architecture. These are the questions we settle before anything ships, and where in the six phases each one gets settled.

docs.h: Who is allowed to see what
docs.t: Whether authorisation resolves per query against the source systems, or the index is partitioned by entitlement. Settled in Foundation, because every later decision inherits it.

docs.h: Who is allowed to see what
docs.t: The version that goes wrong quietly: a pilot built on a manual export, where the permission question was never asked because there was only one copy and one reader.

docs.h: What the system refuses to decide
docs.t: The threshold above which an answer is returned, below which it is escalated, and the path a human sees when it is. Settled in Foundation with the evaluation harness, and measured in Prove.

docs.h: What the system refuses to decide
docs.t: An automation earns trust by knowing what it should not decide. Drawing that line is the work; a disclaimer appended afterwards is not the same thing.

docs.h: What is written down when it runs
docs.t: Which inputs, outputs, model version and decision path are retained, for how long, and who can read them. Settled in Integrate, because retro-fitting an audit trail means re-running history you no longer have.

docs.h: What is written down when it runs
docs.t: This is the evidence procurement and risk ask for after go-live — the question that arrives when something is already in production and nobody captured the answer.

docs.h: Where the data goes, and to whom
docs.t: Which providers process what, in which jurisdiction, whether anything is retained by them, and what leaves your boundary at all. Settled in Frame, because it constrains the architecture rather than following from it.

docs.h: Where the data goes, and to whom
docs.t: For European clients this is the first works-council and procurement question, and it is a design constraint, not a compliance exercise to be run at the end.
What is monitored, what threshold triggers a human, who is on the escalation path, and what the rollback actually is. Settled in Ship, rehearsed rather than theorised.
Models drift, upstream systems change and volumes grow. A system nobody is watching is not governed, however good the policy document is.

docs.h: Who owns it after we leave
docs.t: A named owner, the runbooks, the decision records and the evaluation harness — handed over as working artefacts, not as a folder. Settled in Handover.

docs.h: Who owns it after we leave
docs.t: Governance that depends on the firm that built the system is not governance. It is a dependency.

docs.h: Who owns it after we leave
docs.t: What this page does not claim. Quenora holds no ISO 27001 or SOC 2 certification today, and this page will not imply one. The six decisions above describe how the work is engineered. Attestations, a data processing agreement, subprocessor list and insurance evidence are supplied on request during procurement — ask for them in the first conversation rather than the third.

docs.h: Who owns it after we leave
docs.t: Recognise your own system in any of those five layers? That is the conversation — two paragraphs on which one is stuck.

docs.h: The part most proposals leave out.
docs.t: Every dot is one answer scored against a test set. Without an agreed threshold the spread is just a cloud and any reading of it is defensible. With one, the same cloud splits into shipped, held and escalated — and the argument about whether it worked has a number in it. Illustrative.

docs.h: The part most proposals leave out.
docs.t: “The model is 92% accurate” is not a finding, it is a claim. It becomes a finding when someone else can re-run it next quarter, on new data, and get a number they can compare.

docs.h: The part most proposals leave out.
docs.t: So a Quenora engagement produces a harness alongside the system: the test set, the metric, the thresholds and the script that runs them. It is what Phase 05 measures against, and it is handed over with the code — because the question that matters is not whether the system worked on the day we left, but whether your team can tell six months later that it still does.

docs.h: The part most proposals leave out.
docs.t: It is also the honest answer to a fair objection. A firm with no case studies is asking you to trust an assertion. A firm that hands you the means to check its own work is asking for something much smaller.

docs.h: The part most proposals leave out.

docs.h: A method built to end , not to renew itself.
docs.t: Most consultancies are structured to extend the engagement. This one is structured to finish it — and the process below is designed around that, from the first diagnosis to the deliberate handover.

docs.h: Six phases, fourteen weeks, one handover .
docs.t: Timelines shift with scope — these are indicative, not promises. What does not shift is the shape: diagnose before scoping, demonstrate before integrating, transfer before leaving.

We spend the first weeks understanding what actually happens, not what the process documentation says happens. That means sitting with the people doing the work. That first look is where the constraint nobody mentioned tends to surface.
Exit condition A written position on what to build first — or a recommendation to build nothing.
The data joins, the permissions, the evaluation baseline. This is the layer that decides whether anything later reaches production, and it is the layer most pilots skip.
Exit condition Baseline evaluation scores to judge every change that follows.

Engineering in short cycles against your real systems, with something demonstrable at the end of each. You see working software, not status decks. The person who scoped the work is the person building it.
Exit condition A staged rollout running against real data in a non-production environment.
Into production under the same governance, review and release process as everything else you run — not beside it, and not on an exception.
Exit condition In production, under your existing controls — no exceptions.
Measured against the number agreed in Phase 01, using the evaluation harness built in Phase 02. If it did not move, that is what the written result says.
Exit condition A written result — including the uncomfortable version if that’s the truth.
Documentation, runbooks, architecture decision records, paired operation with your engineers, and a named owner. The engagement is not finished until your team can run it without us.
Exit condition You own it, you run it, we’re gone. That’s the definition of done.

docs.h: Four positions we will not negotiate
docs.t: A rocket booster does not fly alone. A signal booster generates no signal. We attach to the mass you already have — your people, data, processes, market position — and make it go further than it could by itself.

docs.h: Four positions we will not negotiate
docs.t: The people in the room during scoping are the people writing the code. The industry standard of senior partners selling and junior staff delivering is where most of the disappointment in this sector comes from.

docs.h: Four positions we will not negotiate
docs.t: If your deadline is not achievable we say so before the contract is signed. It costs us work in the short term and saves both sides a failed programme in the long term.

docs.h: Four positions we will not negotiate
docs.t: Success is your team running the system without us. We would rather be recommended than retained indefinitely, and the commercial model is built that way on purpose.
